speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
1. The interpretation placed by the joint Federal Appeal Board and Board of Pension Commissioners on section 12 of the Pension Act (as amended 1923) is that a compassionate pension or allowance can only be made where pension has been refused because the death or disability of the member of the forces was due to improper conduct. Even under this interpretation no action towards the award of a compassionate pension or allowance is possible by the joint board on account of the words used in the enactment, viz: "because such case did not form part of any class of case." In the first part of section 12 provision is made for cases arising out of improper conduct consequently they do not form part of a class of case for which no provision has been made. Furthermore, the words "because such case did not form part of any class of case" exclude the interpretation that the discretion vested in the Pension Board is to be exercised by the members of the Pension board and of the Appeal board sitting jointly.

1.	Is the government aware that citizens of the United States who were born in Canada, or who were formerly British subjects, are required to reside in His Majesty's dominions for a period of not less than five years, before they can be repatriated?
2.	Does the government propose to introduce legislation during the present session by way of amendment to the Naturalization Act whereby such citizens may become repatriated in a shorter period of residence than that now required by the act in its present form?

1. Yes. The interdepartmental committee appointed by the Right Honourable M. W. Ridley, Secretary of State for the Home Department, on the 9th of February, 1899, reported on the 24th July, 1901, and dealt with the question of re-admission of denaturalized British-born subjects as follows:
Sec. 35. "We do not think it is necessary to maintain the distinction made in the act of 1870, section 8, between "re-admission" and "naturalization." A person who has become an alien under the provisions of the act must before he or she is qualified for re-admission fulfil the same conditions as are required for
Questions

naturalization. We see no sufficient reason for distinguishing between a statutory and any other alien, and consider that it would tend to the simplification of the law if the provisions of section 8 were repealed and) not re-enacted." This section was, no doubt, considered at the Imperial Conferences which resulted in the approval of The Naturalization Act, 1914.
2. The provisions of the Naturalization Act were settled after discussion at the Imperial Conferences of 1907 and 1911. This legislation is uniform throughout the British Empire, and amendments could be dealt with only after consideration at an Imperial Conference.

speechtext:
The mover of this resolution hopes that before his remarks are concluded the pro forma seconder will be the real seconder. Some days ago we had rather an extended discussion in the House on the subject matter of the Home Bank. The speeches on that occasion were largely delivered in a critical tone, and quite properly so. The purpose of this resolution is to bring to the attention of hon. members of this House some suggestion in the nature of a practical scheme in order that future depositors may be protected better than the depositors have been protected in the past. The purposes of the resolution are as follows:
To provide a definite and practical remedy for the immediate protection of the savings deposits of the great masses of our thrifty citizens.
To re-establish the confidence of the people generally in all our banking institutions.

Savings Bank Deposits
To make possible the continuance of our smaller banks in the field of competition with the larger ones, and thus provide better service to the people of Canada.
To stop the flow of the people's savings into government bonds, government savings banks and long term investments, and to encourage the placing of the people's savings in our chartered banks, where they properly belong, and in this way to assist industry, agriculture, commerce and business in the development of our country.
The whole situation and the general interest of the public with respect to banking conditions in Canada have arisen largely from the merger of, certain banks since the parliamentary committee made their report last year, and that interest has been still more increased by the failure of the Home Bank. It is not my intention to deal extensively, if at all, with that subject, but I would ask hon. members of the House to take the position of the ordinary citizen, and, putting it in a concrete form, I will ask hon. members to journey with me to Fernie, British Columbia, and to go out where the coal company is operating at Coal Creek. Let us take the position of the workingman, the small business man, the thrifty person who wishes to deposit his money in a bank and to have protection. At Coal Creek there was a little building which constituted the office of the company. At one end of the counter in the building was the pay office of the coal company and at the other end was the teller of the Home Bank. There was no other bank or means by which these men could deposit their money unless they went several miles. I will take, not a theoretical, but an actual case of a man who had occupied a prominent position and who had saved $7,200, in order that his daughters, the oldest of whom was sixteen years of age, might be taken from this place which was far in the country to some city where he could give them an education and establish them in the world as any father would like to establish his daughters. He decided, no doubt, to conduct his saving in a thrifty manner. What does the average man do? What, perhaps, did this man do? He sees a sign which tells him something about this particular bank. In glaring headlines he finds that this bank is authorized under the Bank Act to carry on business; that no institution can receive deposits unless it is carrying on business-under the Bank Act. He finds that this bank has a capital authorized of $5,000,000, a capital paid up of $1,960,000 and a rest account of $550,000. Being a careful man, he wants to make further investigations.

How can he do so? He does not understand the returns which are given to parliament and very few men do. He picks off the counter where he is giving his deposits to the bank, the eighteenth annual report of the 31st May, 1923, of the Home Bank of Canada. Let us see what convinces him in this report. He finds first a splendid array of directors and officers. Then there are set out the branches, seventy-eight in number, throughout Canada, this indicating a very large and important institution. Further along he observes that dividends have been paid regularly; that the deposits of the people of Canada have been placed in this institution up to the large sum of $22,000,000, and that is a very great assurance in itself. He finds that the total assets are given at $28,000,000. Still further he looks for the auditor's report, and he finds that this is given pursuant to the Bank Act and the regulations of parliament under law. A portion of this report reads:
The foregoing balance sheet has been examined with the books and vouchers at the head office, and with the certified returns from the branches, and is in accordance therewith	The cash has been checked and the securities of the bank verified, at its chief office, both on the 31st of May, 1923, and also at another time during the year. The cash and securities of one of the branches have also been checked, and in each case they have agreed with the entries in the books of the bank with regard thereto.
Then he turns to the report of the directors and he finds it stated that:
The net profit for the year, after providing for bad and doubtful debts, rebate of interest of unmatured bills under discount, payment of municipal taxes, cost of management, etc., amount to $232,539.17.
The president gives this information. The auditor of this company is Mr. Jones, so the president tells the shareholders that:
Mr. Jones' name will be submitted at this meeting for reappointment as auditor for the ensuing year... It is hoped that the changes enacted will accomplish the objects intended.
He finds that the general manager makes this comment on the solvency and strength of this institution:
But have carried out measures of retrenchment that will inspire additional reassurance for the future.
Finally, the irony of the whole situation is embodied in this resolution of two innocent shareholders:
That the thanks of the shareholders be tendered to the general manager, the assistant general manager and the other officers of the bank for the efficient maimer in which they have respectively discharged their duties during the past year.
My purpose in reviewing that report is this: What has parliament done under the law as it stands to-day, to safeguard an ordinary citizen who takes ordinary precautions to protect

Savings Bank Deposits
his savings? There is not the protection under the law to-day, and protection can be given if parliament is disposed to investigate the matter sufficiently and to provide that protection. In this particular case, what was the situation on the 31st May, 1923? The $550,000 of reserve was wiped out; the $2,000,000 of capital has disappeared; the whole thing can be stated in this way, that the report was a sham, a farce and a crime upon the people of Canada. In my opinion, this should not be allowed to be repeated because we cannot have a second Home Bank failure in Canada. If the government stands aside and appoints royal commissions and waits for something to turn up, we are going to have further complications in our banking institutions and we are going to have public confidence shaken still more than it is to-day. We are going to find the savings of the people drifting across into the United States, taken from our banks and put into government bonds and long-term investments, thereby imperilling and restricting the development of the industry and commerce of this country.
Some days ago when the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) moved this resolution, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) moved an amendment, what one might call a "chloroform" amendment. The intention, according to the Journal, was to thwart and eliminate any investigation or any remedies which might and should be provided. Nevertheless, the amendment was passed.
I wish, at this stage, to repeat one or two observations that I made a few days ago with regard to the centralization of the banking business of Canada. I would ask the government seriously to consider the situation as the facts stare them in the face if they make the most cursory examination of reports which have been given to parliament by the banks themselves. We need not be under any confusion about this. We have the past before us and the present is merely a connecting link between the past and the future. The signs of the times point most decidedly to the elimination of all our smaller banking institutions and the centralization of the banking business in four or five of the largest banks of this country. What are these signs? You need take only the official returns given by the banks each month under the Bank Act and examine those in four or five respects. I have made this examination during the past thirty years. The number of our banks carrying on business under competition in Canada in 1867 was 22; in 1890, 40; in 1900, 36; in 1910, 28; and in 1924, 14. But we must, in fairness to the banking system of this country
-and it is a good banking system as such- admit that banking facilities have been extended by the branches of the banks. In 1890, the banks had 402 branches; in 1900, 663; in 1910, 2,368, and at the end of 1923, they had over 4,400 branches carrying on business and giving service to the people of this country. The capital invested in all the banking business in Canada is as follows:

1900	 67,000,000
1910		 100,000,000
1923'.'		 123,000,000
But while the capital has increased approximately the small extent of 84 per cent from 1900, the volume of business handled by the banks has increased by over 1,100 per cent. In 1900	we	had $1,500,000,000	according to thereturns	and	in	1923	this	had	increased	to
$17,000,000,000. I would call the attention of the House to another significant fact, that while the capital has apparently increased, such a large amount of money has been placed in bank premises and real estate by the banking institutions that the liquid capital in 1923 was only $47,000,000 as against $60,000,000 in 1900 and $74,000,000 in 1910. All these facts are obvious to anyone who will study the situation. Perhaps the most astounding feature of my analysis, which is as accurate as possible, having been checked two or three times, is that out of a total of some $2,000,000,000 of deposits in the banks of Canada not less than 70 per cent are in the hands of the four largest institutions, leaving 30 per cent of deposits to the ten smaller banks that are struggling to exist in the field of competition. That in my opinion is the most amazing, the most important and the most significant feature of all the signs that point towards centralization.
Let us see what the situation has been in the past thirty years. In 1890, 30 per cent of the deposits were in these four largest banks, while 70 per cent were in the other banks. In 1900, 40 per cent were in the four large banks and 60 per cent in the others; in 1910 the proportion stood at 45 per cent in the four and 55 per cent in the others; and in 1923 the percentages were respectively 70 per cent in the four largest banks and 30 per cent in the rest of our banking institutions.

In 1879 the Bankers' Association came to parliament with the request that legislation be passed to give priority to the holders of bank notes against the estate of a defunct bank.

That priority extended not only ahead of all other creditors, but to my know-4 p.m. ledge it is the only instance in which debts due to the Crown take second place. I do not think I can better explain to the House what then took place than by quoting from a little pamphlet, Canadian Banking, written by the late Sir Edmund Walker. It seems to me that in the death of Sir Edmund Walker Canada has lost one of her big men. He was not only a philanthropist, but a patron of art and literature, and he also took a keen interest in education. In a word, he was the type of man that helps to build any country in a real and material way. At page 22 I find the following: Since 1880 note issues have been a prior lien upon the estate of a bank, prior even to a debt due to the Crown. This legislation was prompted by the failure of a small bank in 1879, which did not pay its notes in full. The bankers had urged such legislation in 1869, and if they had succeeded in obtaining it then, we should be able to say to-day that, without further security than this prior lien on all assets, note issues had always been paid in full, no matter how bad the failure of the issuing bank.
Then on the following page this will be found:
And, while it might be confidently asserted that all bank issues secured by being a first lien on the estate of the banks would eventually be paid in full, it was nevertheless true that, because of doubt and delay, the notes of a suspended bank might fall to a discount for the time being. To meet these two defects, the bankers at this time proposed the following new features which were adopted by the government:
1. To avoid discount at the moment of suspension of a bank, either because of delay in the payment of the note issue by the liquidator, or of doubt as to ultimate payment, each bank is obliged to keep in the hands of the government a deposit equal to five per cent on its average circulation, the average being taken from the maximum circulation of each bank in each month of the year. This is called the Bank Circulation Redemption Fund, and should any liquidator fail to redeem the notes of a failed bank, recourse may be had to the entire fund if necessary. As a matter of fact, liquidators are almost invariably able to redeem the note issues as they are presented, but, in order that all solvent banks may accept without loss the notes of an insolvent bank, these notes bear five per cent interest from the date of suspension to the date of the liquidator's announcement that he is ready to redeem.
Sir Edmund Walker refers to the experiences in the United States, and says:

I should like to finish the quotation from Sir Edmund Walker's pamphlet:
That our bank notes are abundantly secured, so far as the public is concerned, seems evident from the fact that a note circulation at 31st December, 1922, of $176,201,351 was in effect secured by a prior lien on total assets of $2,618,638,104, to which must be added the double liability of the shareholders on the capital stock of the banks, making a total of $2,743,930,038. That the banks are not likely ever to lose a dollar by the system of guaranteeing each other's notes seems quite clear. Daily redemption and other features in the act make it difficult to create a forced circulation and, although we have had several fraudulent bank failures, there has never been a case where the assets on which we had the first claim did not easily protect us.
Now my proposal is this: li the bank notes which at any given moment during the period of non-business hours are held chiefly by the banks of the country are so amply and exceedingly well protected, surely parliament in the face of the experiences of the past, and especially in the face of recent experiences, has a duty and a responsibility to protect the man on the street who knows nothing about these matters. Some will say that this proposal is not practicable, that you cannot work out a guarantee system. In fact, I have here a little booklet issued by the Bankers' Association called The Bank Act-Its Audit Provisions and the Suggested Guarantee of Deposits, and the whole substance of the contention in this booklet is a general guarantee of deposits.
I have explained how it was worked out in the United States, where a guarantee of all the deposits was undertaken by each bank guaranteeing the deposits of the others. My proposal is entirely different from that. My proposal is that we build up an insurance fund on a system of premiums by which the citizen who wants mainly protection, who puts

Savings Bank Deposits
his money into the bank so that he may find it there when he wants to draw it out a week or a month or a year from now, will pay a portion of the premium, and the banks also, having increased deposits by reason of thi3 arrangement, will pay a portion of the premium. How does this work out? We have the authority of one of the foremost men perhaps in the world on this particular question, of which he has made a study. In the report of the Comptroller of Currency for the United States, in 1921, at page 20, it is explained:
Full Guaranty of Bank Deposits for $25 per Million of Deposits
During the past six years of stress and strain the losses to national bank depositors from failure have been reduced to such unprecedentedly low figures that an annual charge on all deposits of 2i ten-thousandths of 1 per cent of deposits would have been more than sufficient to cover all such losses accruing to the depositors of our national banks for this period. It is believed that it would be preferable at the outset, as heretofore recommended, to begin with a guarantee of deposit balance of $5,000 or less, and the guarantee plan can then be developed in accordance with the lessons of actual experience.
If the excellent record made by the national banks in the past six years in the matter of immunity from failure should be maintained the government could meet all such losses arising from the guarantee of national bank deposits from 1 per cent of the annual profits which it will receive as a franchise tax from the operation of the Federal reserve banks, if we assume that these reserve banks in the future should only make one-half of the net earnings which they have made in the past 12 months.
No better way can be suggested for bringing into life and getting back into circulation the enormous amount of money which is now hidden and stored away and kept out of banks by timid and nervous owners.
That is exactly the situation in Canada. He continues:	[DOT]
The guarantee of all deposits of national banks of $5 ,000 and less would give complete security for their money to more than 19,000,000 depositors whose deposits in the national banks at this time are estimated at about six thousand million dollars. The remaining individual deposits in national banks, about eight billion dollars, stand to the credit of depositors whose balances exceed $5,000 and those larger depositors aggregate in number, according to the latest estimates, considerably less than 5' per cent of the total number of depositors.
In Canada the deposits on demand, which are saving deposits, amounted on September 30, 1923, approximately to $1,100,000,000, or a little over one billion dollars, so if the same rate were applied in Canada, where according to the best authorities we have fewer failures, the rate of insurance would really be less than it is in the United States, and it would still further be less when you consider that this proposal asks for a guarantee of deposits only up to $3,000, and not for the full amount of the deposits, upon which basis the Comptroller of Currency works out his report.
To summarize, my proposal in short is this: To leave the business of banking with all its intricacies, as it has been built up on experience, exactly as it is. Let the banker's skill and judgment and his responsibility go together. Parliament should not unnecessarily meddle in the complicated business of banking. But in addition to the existing accounts, current and savings, my suggestion is that we create this special class of account so that the man who walks off the street into one of these great pillared institutions and sees the figures across the window showing the bank's capital, but knows nothing about its balance or its solvency, will know that his money will be there when he wants to draw it out a week or a month or a year from now. It is not only the man who does not know much about banking that will take advantage of that class of account. Though that class of account will pay only 2.9 per cent on the money deposited, the depositors' money will be protected, and many people who wish to make deposits will deposit their money in this guarantee account. Others may prefer to put their money in the ordinary bank which they think is safe, and where they will draw three per cent. In this way not only will the depositors have protection, but there will be increased confidence in the banks. The confidence of the people in many of our banks has been shaken, and if we are going to have the smaller institutions remain in business we have to do something, and do it in the near future, in order to retain deposits in these smaller banks, and stop them wandering across into the United States or into our larger banking institutions, or into the Ontario savings office and other institutions throughout the country.
It is perhaps unnecessary for me to point out to the House .that under the Bank Act our chartered banks have very great and very important privileges. They have the exclusive "monopoly of the business of banking. They have the privilege of note issue, on which they earn large sums of money without, you might say, paying anything for it. They have the right of rediscount facilities under the Finance Act, whereby if they are short of capital they may take their securities to the government and say: "Here, we have these securities but we are short of money; you lend us the money on these securities," and the government at once issues notes in accordance with the Finance Act.

Now I do not doubt that hon. members who oppose my motion will show that these facilities are provided by the post office savings bank; that if people want protection for their money they do not need to go to the chartered banks at all. I submit that such is not the case and for these reasons. In the conduct of the post office savings bank business you must appear personally at the post office wicket. There are no checking privileges, you cannot write cheques on the bank, you have got to go there and draw out your money. In British Columbia, for example, you have to file your application and wait until the application goes down to Ottawa, where the money has been deposited, and the funds come back. In other words between the time of your asking for your money and the time of receiving it a period of approximately fourteen days elapses. Furthermore, in the case of the post office savings bank you are only allowed to deposit $1,500 a year and the whole business and machinery connected with the institution is very slow. But there is a much more serious objection to that proceeding than any of those I have mentioned. I contend that it is unsound in principle and is not in the best interest of the country that governments, either federal or provincial, should open savings banks at all. If we had sufficient protection in our chartered banks you would not need to have the provincial and Dominion governments establishing banks from one end of Canada to the other, increasing the rate of interest in order to induce people to put their money into those banks, thereby attracting money from the chartered banks and paralyzing industrial and agricultural activities-because that money in the chartered banks is loaned in the interest of the industrial expansion of the country. The whole principle of these government savings banks is unsound; and for my part I should like to see the post office savings banks, the Ontario savings offices and the Manitoba savings banks offices, entirely wiped out, because that would be in the best interests of the very people that these institutions are intended to serve. Let us suppose, for example that we carried this principle even further than it has been carried. Let us suppose that every province has its savings 
banks as well as the Dominion, and that everybody is invited from motives of selfinterest as well as for reasons of loyalty, upon every ground of sentiment and profit, to put his money into these banks, what would be the consequence? It must be clear as it is possible to demonstrate that to draw the savings from the chartered banks and the banking institutions would leave no money to develop the business and industry of the country. Therefore I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this deposit feature should not be encouraged by this government or by parliament.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) on bringing this all-important subject before the House. I cannot agree with his entire argument, but with part of it I am in complete accord. I intended to quote from a leading article in the Toronto Saturday Night in regard to insuring of deposits. I notice the hon. member who preceded me covered the points to a certain extent, and I will try to omit any repetition of his statements. The article in the Toronto Saturday Night reads:
The main arguments in favour of such a system-
That is the system of insuring deposits-
-according to the United States controller are, that it would bring from hiding places many millions of dollars of hoarded money, a contingency which we now genuinely face; that it would largely prevent runs on the banks, and that such a law would contribute largely to the unification and solidarity of the banking system.
Then it goes on to quote the very small percentage that it would cost to insure such deposits; this figure was given to us by the hon. member who moved the resolution. The article proceeds:
It might be well if the members of the Canadian Bankers' Association discussed seriously the adoption of some such system, for as Mr. Cherry points out in his communication, stable and normal conditions are a prime necessity at this time.
I have been led to understand that banks have been bolstered up by the government for some years, and that hardly a year goes by in which some bank does not request the government to lodge deposits with them to help them through a crisis. I wish to place on record some figures that have been very carefully compiled as to the relation of the Dominion government to chartered banks in regard to deposits, and advances under the Finance Act. These figures relate to 1923 and the statement reads as follows:
A statement of deposits made by the Dominion government in the various chartered banks shows that as deposits were reduced by the withdrawal of deposits by the public from a number of chartered banks in Canada last fall, (particularly the month of October 1923) deposits in these particular banks by the Dominion government were increased.
While this policy was followed in regard to the Dominion, Union, Standard and Sterling Banks, the reverse policy was followed in the case of the Home Bank. To what extent did this policy of the government assist the four banks named, and to what extent did the reverse policy in the case of the Home Bank contribute to the failure of that bank?
In January 1923, taking, the Dominion Bank,
we find they had in current accounts and savings accounts $88,400,000 in that bank.
I will not bother the House with April and July, but I can give the figures if required. 
In October this amount had dropped to $77,-
600,000.	Now let us look at the amount the government of Canada had on deposit in the Dominion Bank in these months. In January it had $1,800,000, and in October it had increased to $6,016,853, and there was due to the Dominion under the Finance Act $2,800,000.
In the case of the Union Bank we find that in the month of January the public had deposits to the extent of $92,900,000. In October that had dropped to $82,200,000. Turning again to the amount the government had on deposit, we find that in January it only had $268,000, while in October it had increased to $1,588,000, and under the Finance Act it had $12,500,000 in addition. In the case of the Standard Bank the same line was followed. In January they had $60,600,000 in public deposits. In October the amount dropped down to $48,100,000. On the other side we find the Dominion government had on deposit only $329,000 in January, but in October they increased the deposit to $8,600,000, while the bank owed under the Finance Act no less than $3,000,000.
Turning to the Home Bank for a moment, in January that bank had of the public's money $18,100,000. In the month of June that had increased to $19,200,000, but as far as the government deposits went, the deposits were decreased instead of increased as in the other cases. In January the government had in the Home Bank $243,000, but when the bank went smash on the 17th August the government had withdrawn these moneys, leaving only $9,000 there. Hon. gentlemen will notice from the aforesaid that when deposits were withdrawn by the public from the Dominion Bank, the Union Bank and the Standard Bank, the Dominion government increased its deposits with them, but in the case of the Home Bank the reverse took place. The public, having confidence in the Home Bank, increased their deposits in January from $18,100,000 to $19,200,000 in June, and when the bank went smash, although the Dominion government had the sum of $243,000 in the Home Bank in January, it had only $9,000 in that bank on the 17th August. The question arises, did the action of the government materially hasten the bank into, liquidation?
In the discussion which took place in this House a few nights ago the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) stated that in his opinion this bank should not have been allowed to go to the wall. It looks very much as if they had intentionally saved the other banks. The question arises:	Why were the
depositors of the Home Bank not helped in the same way as the depositors of the other

banks and that bank kept alive? It is interesting to see what such a conservative paper as the Toronto Saturday Night has to say in an editorial with regard to the present situation of our banks:
The mere fact that a financial institution, manned by several men of eminence in the community, had been enabled to carry on business for years, sell shares and accept deposits, while literally bankrupt and so regarded by the inner circle of financiers, has robbed the community at large of that sense of security which the Canadian banking system was supposed to symbolize. Let it be remembered that last winter when the Bank Act was up for revision, the public received solemn assurances from eminent men that the Canadian system was the best ever devised for the protection of the public; and a few months later were confronted with the spectacle of the rankest failure that has been known in Ontario since confederation. What wonder if the psychological effect has been general distrust?
There was also this aggravating circumstance: The erroneous impression had been abroad that it was now the policy of the Bankers' Association, as a body, to take care of depositors in case one of its members fell by the wayside. This was the general impression gained from replies to critics when the whole question was before the parliamentary committee on banking at Ottawa last session. When this impression proved false, there arose a deep-rooted feeling among vast masses of people that the whole financial community was engaged in a conspiracy against them.
Now it is clear that the Bankers' Association and the Finance department of Canada must get together and do something to restore the public morale... It would perhaps surprise eminent members of the banking profession to learn how many thousands of people to-day believe that the reason they have resisted government inspection is that they have something sinister to conceal.
I have never been able to understand why no encouragement was given to the public at large, to place their savings in post office savings banks. The only reason I can see why more encouragement was not given is because of the intense propaganda put forward in all parts of this country that the present commercial banks were absolutely safe and could take care of or practically guarantee the deposits of the people. I do not understand why-I think it was in 1897- the interest on savings in the post office savings banks was cut down from four to three per cent, unless it was to prevent competition against commercial banks. I cannot understand why the people have not been encouraged to place more money in post office savings banks, particularly when the government has been borrowing continually for its needs. If we had increased the interest from three to four per cent or even to four and one-half per cent when the government was wanting money so badly; it would have been, not only a good thing for the public, but a great saving in the matter of interest to the government itself. Further, I do not understand why a restriction is placed on people using the post office savings banks, why there
should be a limit to the amount of 81,500 per annum, and why, when anyone gets an amount of $5,000 placed in that department he should be refused any more interest. I do not intend to take up the time of the House in going over the unhappy history of what has taken place during this past year. I might, however, refer to these disasters as an orgy of failures. This came as an utter surprise to the people of Canada,' particularly after the intense efforts that were made to remedy various deficiencies in the Bank Act last year, many of those efforts being unfortunately without effect. I should like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the condition that we have gone through in the last eight or nine months was prophesied by a Canadian who had taken a very great interest in the financial life of this country during the past twenty years. I wish to point out the work of a Mr. W. L. Baker, once with the Standard Bank of Canada, who in 1921 issued a book entitled Money Monopoly vs. the Community Dollar in which he drew the attention of the Canadian people to the very serious condition of the banking institutions of Canada and the lack of all guarantees to the savings of the people. Some time before the Home Bank failure took place, the following rather extraordinary editorial came out in the Financial Post on February 23, under the title of Banking and Banking.
Canadian Banks are chartered by the Dominion government, and are operated under strict regulations as
regards their trusts of money deposited by the public, and even in the event of failure there would be no loss to the depositors.
I wish the House to note that.
Shareholders might be expected to face a loss, but not those, who in good faith had placed their money in the keeping of the bank. Statutory provision provides against any such an eventuality.
Mr. W. L. Baker at once replied in the public press, in part saying:
There are no strict regulations, no statutory provisions which make loss to depositors impossible in the event of failure of a bank, and yet this is exactly what the Post says obtains in our Canadian system. There is no legislation which compels the bank to be any more careful in investing the savings of the people than restrictive or protective legislation regarding any phase of banking or banking funds.
The statements, coming out during this session, I am sure, will not only enlighten the people of Canada to the position they are

in, and the inability of the present financial institutions under the present Bank Act to guarantee the savings of the people, but create a demand for some system whereby the thrifty of this country can know that they can be guaranteed that their savings will be looked after. At a later date, again before these financial calamities came upon Canada, Mr. Baker, in writing to the Busy East magazine, made the following statement;
Canada is approaching a serious crisis in her banking business.
I desire to put that on record 'because no credit has been given those who have pre-. dieted the present situation and tried to guard the people against the tremendous losses which have been incurred during the last twelve months. I again express appreciation of the efforts of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), or any other hon. member of this House who may bring forward resolutions with the object of trying to improve the financial institutions of the country. I am entirely in sympathy with his amendment to have this matter go to the committee on Banking and Commerce, and I hope we shall be far more successful than we were a year ago. At any rate, I believe the matter will receive more sympathetic consideration.

I will bring it up at the proper time when I have the opportunity. What I am pointing out is that while this system of receiving deposits at the various offices of the Receiver General in Canada has been discontinued throughout Canada, it still obtains in the Maritime provinces and in British Columbia. The finest note we have in this country is the national note of Canada in one and two dollar bills. These notes circulate everywhere, and in the western provinces within the last few months national notes of five and ten dollars denominations have been .used in the purchase, I believe, of grain and in other ways as well. We have the right to issue those, or larger, notes, but some one put a stop to it and the banks have sub-

Savings Bank Deposits
stituted their notes for them. If the one and two dollar notes are good, why should not the fives, the tens, the fifties and one hundreds be issued in Canadian national notes instead of having bank notes? The bank notes have to be redeemed; and they are not redeemed, as the late president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce stated, by the banks themselves; they are actually redeemed by the money belonging to depositors in these banks. And when a depositor thinks he is going to get his money which he has placed in the bank he finds that a lot of it has been grabbed to take care of notes issued by the bank. That is something that should not continue. In the United States there is only one currency, the national currency; and the best currency in the world to-day consists in the national notes of the United States. The greenback to-day is the greatest note in the world, and next to that is our Canadian national note. We have these notes in circulation in Canada, principally ones and twos, and I see no reason why fives and tens should not be in use as well. That is a question which I should like to have the Banking committee investigate. I may say that we have issued notes of five thousand and ten thousand dollars, but the banks get them by way of discount with the government. Do they put those notes into circulation? Not at all; they deposit them in the Central Gold Reserve in Montreal. This of course is a sound institution, but it is eminently a bankers' institution; and the result of this is that the national notes disappear. They are all burned; and replaced by bank notes which go all over the country. So far these notes have been protected not by the government but by the money placed by depositors in the banks.
Now, I am aware that I am speaking to a very small House, but my voice will carry very much further than the precincts of this chamber, for there are people all over the country who are closely following this question. Let me say therefore that in my opinion the time has come when, first of all, we must modernise the post office savings bank so that the people may have their cheques marked, which cheques, when so marked, shall be legal tender in clearing house transactions. These cheques ought to go through the clearing house, and that I think, should be done on the day the cheque is taken to the bank. As things are at present it takes five days for the cheque to go from Toronto to Ottawa and return, while the period of this delay is ten days in the case of cheques coming from the western provinces. That is an absurd state of affairs. The present Postmaster 77
General (Mr. Murphy), I am told, has in mind a scheme-in fact, I believe he has it in concrete form on his table-for the modernization of the post office savings bank. But we cannot hear anything in reference to this matter. Perhaps we might ask the Acting Postmaster General (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil) whether he knows anything about it, but he too is out of the House and apparently there is no one available to answer this important question.
There is something else I want to tell the public. While we have stopped taking deposits at the various offices of the Receiver General in this country, the United States today is taking deposits, of amounts of up to five hundred or a thousand dollars, payable one year after date with interest at 4 per cent payable half-yearly. So that any man in the United States who does not consider the ordinary banks secure can go to the agency of the national reserve bank system, deposit	anything	up to five hundred	or athousand dollars,	and get a	certificate	whichis practically a bankers' receipt. That receipt is good for the amount deposited,	at 4	per cent,	payable	halfyearly,	the whole payable	within a	year.
Why have we not something like that here? They have a national reserve bank system in the United States. Why should we not have it? They have something like it in the Old Country in the Bank of England. But somebody does not allow these progressive measures to become law here. Although the Bank Act was revised last session any progressive amendments were denied. I may be only a weak voice in this country but I intend to raise these questions before the committee on Banking, namely, as to national notes taking the place of bank notes; as to the establishment of a national reserve bant system similar to that in the United States; and as to public deposits being received by the government. I give the Drury government credit for establishing provincial savings banks in Ontario. Already over $20,000,000 has been deposited by the people in these banks. They have no use for the old-fashioned savings bank account which has been enveloped in so much red tape. Even the Receiver General's offices in Toronto and other cities, which were once doing business and accepting deposits, have been tied up. Who is responsible for this action I do not know. I have raised the question in this House, but without obtaining any satisfactory information. When we get before the committee on Banking we will have it looked into. But there is chloroform all over the country, it is even in this House,

and neither the present Minister of Finance nor his predecessor is here when the question of our banking system comes up for discussion.

The public are entitled to protection similar to that proposed in this resolution. Anyway, something has to be done, and parliament and the government must take action to afford relief to the public. There is a national currency in nearly all other countries, but for some reason or other in this progressive Dominion we cannot have even a modernized system of post office savings banks.
And yet I have not any great fault to find with our chartered banks. They are giving great service to the public and they are making money in doing so. But they have great privileges, and some of these privileges must be regulated. Undoubtedly there must be security afforded the public by instituting a proper system of bank auditing.

I point out to
the Prime Minister that when this question comes up in connection with our banking laws he does not happen to be in his seat, and his Minister of Finance is also absent. Of course, the Prime Minister is only responsible for what occurs during his term of office-and he did not draft the Bank Act. But I should like to know from him why we have not got a national currency; why the Receiver General's offices in Toronto and other cities, which some years ago received deposits from the people and paid them out on demand,-why these offices have been closed in Ontario and Quebec while they have been continued in the Maritime provinces and British Columbia.
After listening to the arguments presented by the two previous speakers, I say it is high time that this House approached the question of banking reform. We had it up last session, but the Bank Act was passed with very few improvements in it. Fortunately the question is coming up again this session, and I hope the government will take the lead in some measure of reform. But that reform must be in the direction I have stated. For instance, we must have a national currency in the place of bank note currency which, when a bank fails now, is redeemed by the deposits of the people. When a depositor goes to withdraw his money he is told, "Your deposit is weakened by our having to cash in for bank notes that the defunct bank issued." That should not be allowed to continue. There should be an absolute reliable national currency as good as gold, just as there is in the States.

They have a national note there; we got it only in part. What is good enough for Uncle Sam is good enough for Jack Canuck. We want the same law in re-

gard to the post office savings banks. I hope now I have had the opportunity of presenting these ideas to the Prime Minister that we shall get some assurance from him that this question will go to the Banking committee, and that the Banking committee will take up the question of banking reform, including the substitution of national currency for bank currency, the opening of the Receiver General's office as a place for deposits, and the modernizing of the post office savings bank making it just as convenient for the ordinary depositor as the ordinary savings bank. All the modernization it needs is that the depositor can go to a post office savings bank and get his cheque marked and stamped; and when stamped that will go through the clearing house of all the banks at par.

Mr. Speaker,
with much of what the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) has said I am in agreement, but I would not like to endorse everything that he has said in connection with his motion. I believe, however, that the subject matter is of very great importance, and that it ought to receive the careful consideration of the Banking and Commerce committee. It is very significant indeed that when the act was under consideration last year in the committee and in the House, Mr. Baker, who has been referred to by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) published a letter in the Ottawa Citizen, which has been already alluded to. I would like to quote one or two paragraphs from that letter in addition to the one quoted by the hon. member for Battle River. His letter contains an enumeration of the lack of safeguards then existing in our banking legislation. Mr. Baker says:
There is no law restricting the amount which may be loaned to directors or to firms or companies controlled by directors.
That, I believe, was somewhat modified last year. Continuing:
There is no maximum amount fixed by legislation which may be loaned to any one customer.
There is no law stipulating that the bank shall hold any security for loans or that any percentage of its loans shall be secured.
77i
There is no distinction made between shareholders' funds, commercial deposits and the savings of the thrifty. The banks enjoy unusual privileges in the handling of deposits as "savings banks."
I may comment upon that, that these difficulties or'defects in the pre-existing legislation are those which the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver South is designed to meet. There is no doubt at all that the matter is worthy of the most serious consideration. Continuing from Mr. Baker's letter:
There is no legal requirement regarding the amount of cash reserves a bank shall carry, and possibly no sound reason why there should be, but other countries have such laws, and the fact that we do not, is mentioned merely to show the absurdity of the Post's claim that we have statutes which would provide for such an eventuality as a bank being able to lose for its depositors.
There is no law to prevent any bank from wrecking itself by over-expansion, injudicious banking and permitting the bank's funds to be used in the speculations of a favoured clique, and no limits placed that would make shareholders alone the sufferers.
How we have seen these warnings fulfilled since the 1st of July last! Continuing:
There is no law providing for either government or external inspection. We have shareholders' audit- the sop given to quiet public clamour for government audit, and anyone who studies the act providing for this delusion must recognize what a farce can be made of it.
Mr. Baker goes on to say:
It is high time that the independent press of Canada should give the public real information on a subject of such vital importance and see to it that mutual admiration societies are not left entirely free to spread propaganda for the continuance of a system and policy which may lead to ruin.
I will not read the rest. I quote this to show that men who had an intimate knowledge of the banking situation gave timely warnings last year to have effective safeguards put in our act, but those who attended the committee know how impossible it was even to get adequate discussion of these matters, much less get any necessary amendment put through. The situation, however, is somewhat different this year, and I take it that he will be a brave man who will prevent the calling of witnesses or prevent discussion of these matters this year.
I have here a little pamphlet which I presume has been sent to all the members, written by a certain W. R. Morson, of Toronto. I do not know the gentleman, but I presume he is a man with some banking experience. The pamphlet is entitled A Better Banking System for 'Canada, and here is a very significant statement on page 2:

As an instance of the inefficiency of the present system, take the glaring cases of the Merchants Bank and the Home Bank. The circumstances that finally brought the Home Bank into insolvency were known to many people, myself included, five years ago.
I would like the Minister of Finance to note that. Here is a man who states that he knew the situation five years ago, but our Department of Finance that is supposed to keep track of these things apparently did not know it; or if they did they took no steps to protect the depositors. Continuing:
Tt is not conceivable that those irregularities could have continuned so long under an independent audit and an independent scrutineer.
Further on under a section devoted to the guarantee of deposits he says:
With a proper inspection and power to correct abuses, it would be a perfectly safe undertaking to guarantee deposits. The Controller of the Currency at Washington has shown that the percentage of losses compared to deposits amounted to 1-2400th of 1 per cent per annum for six years previous to 1920, during which period the Federal Reserve was in operation.
I will not read the rest because this is probably not the time and place to enter into a detailed discussion of this matter. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I simply want to repeat my conviction that this question did not receive sufficient consideration last year; that if we are going to prevent this country from going through very, very serious times in the future, more serious I think than we can now imagine, we have got to grapple with some of the real problems that face us in this connection. I have very great pleasure indeed in supporting the amended resolution to refer this particular proposal to the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce.

I thought either the word "protected" or "guaranteed" was used. Now had this matter not been referred already to a committee, as I think it was so referred by the resolution of the 27th March, I do not know that I would be prepared to support the resolution, not because I am opposed to any principle which will assist depositors but because I am more or less opposed to a principle which will involve banking to a very serious extent indeed. The principle of guarantee of deposits, no matter how it may be taken- whether it may be taken by way of a guarantee fund, or whether the guarantee only extends up to a certain amount-cannot stop at the mere question of guarantee. It involves not only the question of guarantee itself, that one item in banking, but it must go down the line into the various banking transactions and more or less involve the principle of banking which we have in this country to-day. I think as my argument develops to some extent hon. members will see that. As a matter of fact the system of guarantee-in any form in which we discuss it or desire to place it before ourselves or a committee-is nothing more or less than a contract or .surety issued. It means that someone else becomes the guarantor of or surety for the principal debtor, the principal debtor in this case being the bank whose deposits are guaranteed.
This sort of guarantee of deposits, I must admit is very attractive looking. It has, particularly at this time, an appearance that merits the most careful consideration. I do not deny that at all, but I do not think we should be led away by a matter of looks or

Savings Bank Deposits
the name which we bestow on any proposal during this discussion. Perhaps we have on other occasions been led away by a system which we think may carry out, or is even certain to carry out, what we expect it to do under the terms of a resolution which has been adopted by the House. But if we look further and if we try and put that system into operation we will discover there are a great many difficulties which occur in connection with the actual law as put into force. Therefore I say I think we should discuss this matter in a dispassionate manner. I think we should not entirely fix our minds on the word "guarantee" alone and think that by reason of that guarantee being effected it is going to accomplish, or will accomplish, the object which is intended. That I may say, Mr. Speaker, is simply a preliminary remark I have to make, and I make it merely because I am trying to discuss this matter purely with an open mind, not with a view to opposition and at the same time to lay stress on what I state, that the question of a guarantee of deposits does not end with the guarantee of deposits alone but goes a good deal further.
Now, in most matters of banking, in most matters of law, in a great many other commercial affairs in life, we attempt in so far as we can to find various precedents to which we can look for experience. We are not altogether bound by precedents. We are not bound to say that a precedent which happened in this country or in that country is what might happen in this country if it were applied here, we are not bound to accept what actually did occur in other places; nevertheless in law, or in commerce, or in other walks of life, the question of what has happened under similar circumstances, is of importance because we are bound to learn from what did occur in other countries something that will be of assistance to us. We have got no precedent in this country as regards the guarantee of deposits direct or indirect. We have no such principle as to the guarantee of deposits direct or indirect by an insurance fund, or otherwise, in any of the great countries of Europe. We have no such precedents so far as I know-and I think I am right in making this statement- in Great Britain on whose system our banking system is based. We have no precedents to which we can look-if I mistake not, and I think I am quite right in making this assertion-in any of the great eastern states. We have, however, precedents in certain of the other states to which we can look and from which we can ascertain whether the system of guarantees turned out successfully
in those states or not. I am not one of those who look to the United States for precedents, I must quite admit. I very much prefer to look for precedents	to Great
Britain.

My hon. friend is not quite right in his statement. The guarantees which took place in the United States were not all limited. Some were limited, some were voluntary and some were involuntary. As regards the insurance principle for the
Savings Bank Deposits

guarantee of deposits which my hon. friend brings up, I will explain to him in a few moments that I have not forgotten what he stated in regard to the insurance principle, but I want to make my point absolutely clear in discussing the guarantee of deposits, and I am perhaps going more or less ahead of the argument I intended to make, but I want to make abundantly clear-and I might as well do it now-that if there is to be any guarantee at all it must be such a guarantee that there need be no explanation behind it, that anybody going to any bank and placing deposits there will know definitely and absolutely that if that bank fails these deposits will be paid. That is the only kind of guarantee that is worth anything. I do not care what is behind that guarantee, I do not care what is in front of it, and I do not care what conditions surround that guarantee. What I say is this -and I repeat it because it is a most important point in connection with this guarantee

that if any guarantee of bank deposits exists at all, it must be such that the poor man, the rich man, or whoever the man may be, and no matter in what bank he places his money, will know that if that bank fails that money is to be paid without any legal argument or without any conditions surrounding it, and that he will receive his money in a short time, without any legal entanglement.

I cannot prophesy that
they will always be paid in full. All I can say is that the system in force at the present time is a fair and reasonable one. I am giving my opinion now on the subject of guarantees and I say that if there is a guarantee at all it must be a good one, not a half or a quarter guarantee. It must be known that the guarantee is actually a guarantee which is worth something. I was going on to speak of certain instances which have happened in the United States and certain precedents which have been established there. There is the case of the state of Oklahoma one of the newer states I admit, but one of the first states to adopt a system of guarantee. It came about somewhat in this way. In 1907, hon. gentlemen will remember, the United States was going through more or less of a period of financial panic. A number of banks had failed. It was the year after the national election. Happily or unhappily in that election Mr. William Jennings Bryan, who was a candidate for president, placed in his platform as a principal plank the promise that there should be a guarantee of all deposits in the banks. I think that was a pretty good card politically. If Bryan had been elected president and the government had guaranteed the deposits in all the banks, it would have been a fine thing. At least, it was an admirable thing for him to say before the election that he was going to try and do it. What he would have done if he had been elected of course, is quite another story .

speechtext: I wish to correct my hon. friend. I did say what it would be. I said it would be built up on the insurance principle, on an actuarial basis founded on experience, exactly in the way insurance companies build up their business. speechtext:
I quite understand that
my honourable friend wants to get at a guarantee system more or less along the lines of insurance, on an actuarial basis or something of that description. It sounds supremely simple, so simple that one might almost imagine that you could sit down at one of these desks and work it out. But I want to revert again to the question which I brought up with my hon. friend, namely, that if he has a system of bank guarantee of deposits, it cannot stop at a guarantee, it will go down into all the intricacies of banking. If he will have a little patience, I shall get into the subject much more quickly. I will not go on detailing all these cases which took place in the United States, although they are of interest. I must admit that the precedents which they show under the experiences which they had at the time were of considerable interest. I was, however, speaking about Oklahoma, under which state this law of joint and several guarantees was adopted. When that guarantee law was passed in the state of Oklahoma, it applied to state banks, not to national banks. It looked at first blush like a very good arrangement for the guarantee of deposits. It also looked like a very good card for attracting deposits to banks. Hence, because of the
apparent power of this system to attract deposits, many banks which were national banks, to which the guarantee law did not apply, turned themselves into state banks. A few of the state banks in the larger cities, being afraid of the guarantee law, turned themselves into national banks. Consequently, it was interesting to ascertain what happened owing to this transition from state banks into national banks. What happened was this. You will remember that the law was passed in 1907. Out of one thousand state banks, in July, 1923, 450 were still in existence; 255 had withdrawn from the guarantee banks turning themselves into national banks; 125 had consolidated with others: 125 had failed, and 50 had been liquidated. That is what happened to the banks that turned themselves from national banks into state banks in order to come under the law of the joint and several guarantee. In 1922, the state of Oklahoma repealed this law, because sound bankers went to the legislature and stated that if the law was to be kept in force, they would have to go out of the banking business entirely or turn themselves into national banks. That repeal of the law which took place at that time at th^, request of prominent bankers took place because there was knowledge that a million dollars was outstanding and unpaid by reason of this particular guarantee fund.
I am going too quickly because I want to explain briefly what happened during the time this guarantee was in effect. As regards depositors, the effect of the guarantee was this:	The law went into effect in February,
1908. At first blush the effect of this law was good. A great mass of deposits flowed into the banks of Oklahoma. As a matter of fact, deposits came not only from this new state of Oklahoma which was a few months old, but from neighbouring states, so much so that the neighbouring states had themselves to make laws guaranteeing deposits, but those neighbouring states did not make their laws in such wise that the guarantee was a several and joint guarantee but they made their laws on the fundamental principle of the law of suretyship. What was this test of the law of guarantee in the state of Oklahoma? The test came along very quickly. The law went into effect in February, 1908, and in May, 1908, three months later, came the first test of this law. The test was only a 'little one; it did not amount to very much. A little bit of' a bank called the International Bank of Coalgate closed its doors. It may have closed its doors in order to put to a test this law of guarantee which the state of Oklahoma had passed. As soon as it closed its doors, state

Savings Bank Deposits
officials walked into the bank, counted the cash, said that there was so much cash there, put the cash aside, put their hands into the till of the guarantee fund and took out of that fund sufficient money to pay all the depositors. That sounds like a very simple procedure; it may sound to hon. gentlemen like a very proper procedure; but it was a most improper procedure under a most vicious principle. The law of suretyship of which this is a part-and it does not matter how it is argued by way of a guarantee fund-is that a contract of suretyship means simply that the principal debtor, that is to say the man or person or corporation owing the money, has first to have his assets and liabilities discussed, his assets sold, the money from those assets brought together, and as regards any deficiency there may be, the surety or guarantee fund, as the case may be, is liable for the difference. That is the ordinary law of suretyship.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is of a legal mind.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I do not know that I am.

Surely the contract of
surety is expressed in the terms of the document. You make it as you want it. You make it fit the situation. You do not adopt some general principle like that, a general scheme under which there is an unlimited call on banks.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
My hon. friend, to some
extent, is quite correct. I am glad that he has brought that question up. No, the general law of suretyship, as I have explained it, is the customary law of suretyship.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: That is not this case.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
My hon. friend is quite
right in what he states that these benefits or advantages which the suretyship may ask for can be limited or not. You can make the contract of suretyship pretty much as you want it, so that the principal debtor may not or will not have to be discussed. That is quite true; but the point which I make is this, that people who have guarantees of deposits do not want to discuss the question of the law at all. I reiterate and repeat that if a bank has written up on its windows "Deposits in this bank are guaranteed," when that bank fails, the people want to know that their deposits are assured, quite irrespective of any intricacies of the law of suretyship or anything else.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Might I ask without anticipating my hon. friend's development of his subject, whether he has any definite proposal by which they can have an absolute assurance of that kind?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I must admit that, although I have studied this question to quite an extent, I have great difficulties in mind in seeing how a guarantee fund could be brought about so that it would actually guarantee deposits. Perhaps if the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) will allow me to progress a little more, I will try to get through immediately. Some questions may develop which will be of use in discussing this subject before the Banking and Commerce committee, because without' a doubt it will be discussed before that committee under the resolution of the 27th of March, and I must say to my hon. friend that I feel a good deal of hesitation in detaining this House in discussing this matter at all, unless what I say is of some particular interest.
Following on the question of what happened in the Oklahoma situation, I will come very quickly to. the conclusion. In October 1909, or two years after the law was passed, another large bank failed, the Columbia Bank and Trust Company. That bank had procured very large deposits owing to the fact that this guarantee fund existed. The directors and officers, having secured these various funds, went into rash speculations and the bank failed, with the result that in 1914-to make a resume of the situation-there had been paid out of the guarantee fund $4,000,000, while there were outstanding unpaid warrants for $1,000,000 more. In 1921 the banks began to fail rapidly and many of those who were in this particular guarantee fund withdrew from it. In November of that year, on the closing of one of the banks, the guarantee fund was bankrupted. In July 1922, there was $3,000,000 out against the guarantee fund, and the fund became bankrupt.
Now, I do not think that this is entirely the question which my hon. friend wants to have settled, but it is a question of a joint and several guarantee fund which I claim the banks would have to enter into in this country in order to make an absolutely positive guarantee.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
think that any member of this House would

seriously propose that, with the system of banking we have in this country, the very large amount of deposits in Canada should be entirely guaranteed? I think his arguments are wide of the mark.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
That is precisely what
the hon. member wants.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
No. If I understand
the proposal of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner), it is that there should be a certain limited class of guaranteed deposits. I do not understand him to propose that all deposits should be guaranteed.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
I am glad my hon.
friend interjects an explanation. Will the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) tell us how he will guarantee deposits limited, say, to $3,000? Will he not create a preferred class of depositors? WTould a man not divide up his deposits, in any case, so that they would all come within the guarantee? Surely my hon. friend does not imagine for a moment that a man who had $10,000 or $20,000 would be foolish enough not to see to it that the whole amount was guaranteed, and not the first $3,000. In the goodness of my hon. friend's heart, and knowing human nature as he does, I think he would admit that people would separate their accounts, put them in different banks, in trust accounts, and under various names, all for the purpose of coming within the $3,000 guarantee. I think that this is almost a frivolous point to raise.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
As the hon. member puts
the matter in that way, I trust he will give me the privilege of making one observation. Apparently he is as far from appreciating the points of my remarks as he is, in his argument, from answering this point I have raised. I do not say that there should be a total guarantee. The deterrent against putting moneys into special accounts would be the fact that they would receive not the regular 3 per cent rate but less than that. In other words, any one who resorted to the means which my hon. friend suggests would have a special reason for doing so, whereas many people would take advantage of the larger interest offered the other way.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I simply wanted to make myself clear, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: The hon. member must not make a second address.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I still regret that I cannot agree with the hon. member. He cannot by the widest stretch of the imagination convince me or any banker, or any person in this House who has not an inhuman character, that if a man has $15,000 and wants to have the whole of it guaranteed he will not be able to do so by separating his accounts and segregating his deposits in different banks, even though, instead of securing 3 per cent, on his deposits, he might get only 2f or 2i per cent. So that it is utterly impossible to fix any guarantee up to a certain amount. But in any event, I say that if a guarantee is to exist it should be a full guarantee, so that every one will be treated alike. Let us say, for the sake of the argument, that only those accounts up to $3,000 will be guaranteed. Does my hon. friend realise what percentage of deposits in the banks comprises accounts of $3,000 and under? No doubt he knows what the figure is.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Not exactly.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Let me tell him: 85 per cent of the deposits in the banks consists of accounts of $3,000 and under.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Has the hon. member any authority for that statement? I have authority for the statement that it is only 55 per cent.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: On inquiry of very prominent bankers I have received the information which I have given. It may be right or wrong but I leave the matter to the judgment of my hon. friend. I am inclined to think, however, that it is right.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
It is not a matter of
guessing.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: No, it is not; and I think the figure I have given is more or less right.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
At any rate, it is a safer
guess than the hon. gentleman's.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: I do not see how my hon. friend (Mr. Ladner) could possibly work out the proposal in regard to a guarantee to the extent of $3,000, and I have indicated one of the difficulties which would supervene in the matter.	.

Will the hon. member
tell us why a man who had $100,000 in the bank should not be as fully protected as the man with $3,000, simply because they were in different walks of life?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Is the question addressed to me?
Savings Bank Deposits

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: It is addressed to hon. members generally.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: The answer is simple. There is no doubt that the man who had $100,000 would see to it that he was guaranteed, and he would be foolish if he did not. I agree with the implication conveyed in my hon. friend's question; I always agree with the hon. member for Hants. Now, as the hour is drawing to a close I think I shall bring my remarks to a conclusion. What I wanted to bring to the attention of the House, as regards these instances in the United States, was the fact that there was a joint and several guarantee of the banks- both an individual guarantee and a partial guarantee-all of which have proved unsuccessful. I do not say for a moment that in this country they might prove unsuccessful also, but we have the evidence of what occurred in the United States. Without a doubt they have not been successful in any single state of the union where these guarantees have existed. Furthermore, not only have they been most unsuccessful from a banking point of view, but they have been equally unsuccessful from the point of view of depositors and of business men generally. There is not a single shred of evidence to show that any of these guarantees which took place in the United States were of any value whatever.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Now that the hon. member has dealt with the states that had guarantees which failed to satisfy the requirements of the guarantee law, will he not tell the House about the guarantee law of the state of Kansas?

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR PROTECTION OF SPECfAL SAVINGS ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Certainly, I will be very
glad to tell the House of the guarantee law of the state of Kansas. It was a voluntary system. Certain banks agreed to enter into the guarantee fund. They created what was called a "guarantee fund account." When a bank failed in Kansas under that guarantee law the depositors were not paid out of the guarantee fund as they were in the Oklahoma case which I cited, but they were given certificates of deposit. It meant that the assets of the bank which had failed had first to be sold. Then the depositors came forward with their certificates of deposit and called upon the guarantee fund for the money that was there to pay those particular deposits. This is what actually happened in 
the state of Kansas. Certificates of deposit had been issued to the extent of over $5,500,000 this is the last report which I could find
and there was in the guarantee fund about $850,000 in cash, and bonds at par of $1,140,000, making a total of $2,000,000, against the payment of guarantee certificates outstanding of $5,500,000.
